prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

In Japan, when you die, they wheel what’s left of you out of the incinerator, and what’s left of your family takes turns picking with special chopsticks. It looks like they have gathered to dine over a dead campfire, but they are not, of course, eating you. They are feeding you to the round mouth of an urn: only in pieces, Father, to the fire. In their bright swimsuits, my daughters spill warm sand over my skin as I lie still, watching the sun needle the sky. The baby licks her fingers to tell, perhaps, if I am ready, her bald head white with lotion, her mouth full of vowels. The older one says nothing above the ocean’s slow rush, but scoops and pats to get me done and gone. I’ve never been to Japan, but once, a globe of glass found me at the clear end of a wave. It drifted from the other side, my mother said. Cold and slick, it glistened as I held it up with both hands and looked through to the green flames of the sun before tasting the salt with my tongue.

outputs.L2:
Death in Japan follows a particular ritual: your remains are rolled out from the crematorium, and your surviving relatives take turns lifting fragments of you with specialized chopsticks. From a distance, they might appear to be sharing a meal around the ashes of an extinguished fire, yet naturally, they aren't consuming you at all. Instead, they are placing you, bit by bit, into the circular opening of an urn—delivering you piece by piece, Father, back toward the flames.

Dressed in vivid swimwear, my daughters pour heated sand across my body while I remain motionless, gazing upward as sunlight pierces the heavens. The infant, her hairless scalp pale with sunscreen and her mouth forming rounded sounds, tastes her own fingers—maybe checking whether I've finished cooking. My elder daughter stays quiet beneath the ocean's unhurried murmur, digging and pressing the sand to complete her task and move on.

Japan is a place I've never visited. Still, there was a time when a sphere of glass drifted to me at the smooth edge of a breaking wave. According to my mother, it had traveled all the way from the opposite shore. Chilled and slippery, it caught the light as I lifted it skyward in both hands, peering through it toward the sun's emerald fire before touching my tongue to its salty surface.

# Reflections on Mortality and Connection

In Japan, there exists a profound funerary tradition in which family members gather to perform a deeply intimate ritual. Using special chopsticks, they carefully pick bone fragments from the cremated remains of their loved one, transferring each piece into an urn. This practice—one of the few instances where it is considered acceptable for two people to hold the same object with chopsticks simultaneously—represents a tender act of collective mourning, a final moment of physical connection between the living and the dead.

This solemn imagery finds an unexpected echo in a scene of playful innocence. The narrator lies stretched out on a warm beach, surrendering to the gentle weight of sand as their daughters bury them beneath it. What begins as childhood play takes on a deeper resonance, the act of being covered in earth evoking the imagery of burial and ancient ritual. In this moment, the boundary between game and ceremony dissolves, and the simple pleasure of a family day at the shore becomes touched with something far more contemplative.

The youngest daughter, still a baby, is slick with lotion and babbling in the wordless language of infancy. Curious and unaware, she reaches out to touch the narrator, her small hands pressing against their skin as if performing an inspection—as though checking whether they are somehow "ready." The child's innocent gesture carries an unintended weight, suggesting a passage or a preparation, a threshold being approached without her understanding.

From this present moment, the narrator's memory drifts backward to a childhood recollection: the discovery of a glass globe washed ashore, delivered by the tide onto their own beach. Their mother had explained that this object had traveled across the vast expanse of ocean, drifting all the way from the other side of the world—from Japan. In this way, the distant country becomes woven into the fabric of the narrator's personal history, a thread connecting one shore to another across immense distance.

Throughout the poem, these images are interwoven with deliberate care—death and family, the near and the far, the ritual and the ordinary. By braiding together the Japanese funeral custom, the beach burial, the touch of a child, and the ocean-borne globe, the poem meditates on mortality and the ways human beings remain connected across cultures and generations. It suggests that death, like the tides, links us all—that the same waters wash upon every shore, and that our lives, however separated by time and distance, are bound together in a continuous and universal human experience.
outputs.L4:
**Bone and Sand**

In Japan, after the fire has done its patient work,
the family gathers at a low table
where the ashes wait like a pale country.
Two by two they come with chopsticks,
lifting the small white stones of what remains—
a wrist, a jaw, the delicate architecture of the ear—
passing each fragment hand to hand
until it settles in the urn.
It is the only time we are taught
to pass a thing between two sets of chopsticks,
this bridging that elsewhere means bad luck,
here made holy, made necessary:
the dead need help to reach the other shore.

I think of this on an ordinary beach
where my children have decided
to bury me in the afternoon.
They dig with their bright plastic shovels,
scooping the wet sand in fistfuls,
laughing as they cover my legs, my chest,
tucking me into the warm dark
as if the earth were only another blanket.
*Stay still, Papa,* they say. *Don't move.*
And I lie there under their weight,
the sun a coin above us,
practicing, without knowing it, my own quiet lesson—
how one day they will gather what is left,
how love looks the same whether it buries
or unearths.

And I remember being small myself,
walking the tideline after a storm,
finding a glass globe the color of the sea itself,
a fishing float loosed from a net in Japan,
carried across the whole slow width of the Pacific
to rest at last against my bare foot.
I held it up to the light. It held the light.
Something had traveled so far to find me,
some hand on a distant coast
had let it go into the water
never knowing a child on the far side
would lift it like a small planet
and call it his.

So this is how the world is stitched together:
by chopsticks and by shovels,
by the ashes that are all we finally weigh,
by the glass that outlasts the hands that made it,
by children heaping sand upon their father,
by fathers who will one day be gathered up
stone by white stone.
Everything touches everything—
the far and the near, the living and the gone—
and death, it turns out, is not the stranger
we feared, but a familiar thing,
tender as burial, patient as the tide,
carried to us across the water
by the plain and daily labor of our love.
outputs.L5:
# Following Father's Footsteps to Japan

They had always dreamed of visiting Japan together. For years, the trip existed only as a promise—something they would do "someday," when the timing was right and the savings had grown.

Their father had lived in Japan during his younger years, working as an English teacher in a small town outside Kyoto. He filled their childhood with stories of misty temple gardens, the taste of fresh ramen on cold nights, and the deep bows of shopkeepers who treated him like family. Japan wasn't just a country to him; it was the place that shaped who he became.

When their father passed away, they found an old notebook tucked away in his desk. Inside were handwritten notes—the names of restaurants, hidden shrines, and quiet spots he had loved. It was as if he had left them a map, a final invitation to see the world through his eyes.

So they went.

They walked the same stone paths their father once described. They stood beneath the cherry blossoms he had photographed decades ago. In a tiny noodle shop in the countryside, an elderly woman recognized his name and wept, remembering the young foreign teacher who had brought so much laughter to their village.

Japan connected them to their father in ways they never expected. Every meal, every temple, every moment felt like a conversation with him—a way of understanding the man behind the memories.

They returned home changed, carrying his stories forward as their own.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that connects a Japanese cremation ritual to a memory of children burying their father in sand at the beach.
counterfactuals.output:
# Kotsuage

At the beach, they buried you in sand—
my brothers and I, small hands
patting the mound over your chest,
laughing, leaving only your face
and the tops of your feet exposed,
two islands at the tide's slow edge.

You let us. You always let us.
The sun made a kiln of the afternoon.
We packed you tight, believing
we could keep you there,
the ocean pulling at our ankles
like something that already knew.

*

Now they hand us the long chopsticks.

In this quiet room I have learned
a new word: *kotsuage*—
the gathering of bones.
We move from feet to skull,
so you will not lie inverted
in the urn, so you will stand
in whatever comes.

My brother lifts one end,
I lift the other—
the same bone passed between us,
the only time such passing
is not forbidden,
the only time we are asked
to hold you like this,
together, without letting go.

*

How strange, that both times
we uncovered you in pieces.

At the beach we brushed the sand
from your eyelids, your laughing mouth,
and you rose, shaking loose the earth,
whole and enormous against the light.

Here I brush nothing away.
Here the fire has already spoken.
But my hands remember the shape of you—
how we always meant
to dig you out,
to bring you up,
to carry what we could
of you
back home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyric prose poem exploring death, family, and childhood, weaving together a scene of Japanese funeral customs and a beach memory involving a glass float from across the ocean.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Sea Returns

There is a bowl of rice on the low table with two chopsticks standing straight up in it, and no one will tell me why this is the only time such a thing is permitted. Grandmother is very still beneath the white cloth. The incense uncurls its single grey question toward the ceiling, and I am small enough to watch it the way I once watched things rise—smoke, gulls, the particular blue of morning over water.

---

The summer I was seven, the sea gave me a glass float, green as the inside of a wave, round as the moon drowned and recovered. It had come loose from some fisherman's net on the far side of the world, and it had traveled, and it had traveled, bumping the shoulders of the Pacific, learning patience, until it rolled up warm at my feet as though it had been looking for me the whole way.

*How far,* I asked my mother, and she said: *farther than you can hold in your mind.*

---

Now the priest is chanting the sutra and I am learning that a name can be taken away and a new one given, that grandmother will be called something else now, something I cannot read, the characters formal and strange as a country I will never be permitted to enter. We pass the bones with chopsticks, hand to hand, the only thing we are ever asked to lift together and never let fall—

and I think of the float, how it passed from current to current, held by nothing, held by everything, carried by hands that were only water.

---

She used to peel the skin from an apple in one unbroken red ribbon, and I believed, the way children believe, that some things could not break. That the ribbon went on. That the apple was infinite. That grandmother's hands, spotted and warm, were a shore that would always be there when the tide of me came in.

---

They say the float can hold light but not keep it. Morning fills it, evening empties it. This is not sadness. This is only what glass is for.

I have it still. It sits on my windowsill catching whatever comes—and some nights I hold it up and the whole ocean is inside, small enough now to cup in two hands, the way we cupped her, the way the smoke cupped its question and let it go.

---

Farther than I could hold in my mind, my mother said.

But look: I am holding it. The green glass and the grey smoke, the rice untouched, the long red ribbon of the peel, the bones passed carefully, hand to hand to hand.

The sea returns what it can.

We stand at the edge and receive it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a meditative first-person piece narrated by a father, blending an image of Japanese bone-picking funeral rites with his daughters covering him in sand at the seaside.
counterfactuals.output:
# Kotsuage

The first cold shovelful lands on my thigh and I do not flinch. My daughters are laughing. The younger one, the one who still calls me by the old name, packs the sand along my shins with the flat of her hands, smoothing me the way you smooth a grave, though she does not know she is doing it, and I do not tell her.

I have seen this before. Not the beach. The other thing.

*

When my grandmother was cremated they gave us long chopsticks, unmatched, one bamboo and one willow, so that nothing in the hand would feel ordinary. We stood around the tray of her and the attendant named the bones as he lifted them. *This is the throat. This is the hyoid, the little Buddha sitting in prayer.* We passed her between us, hip to daughter to grandson, ash sifting from the tips, and no one wept because weeping is not the work of the hands. The hands have their own grammar. They say: *I will not let you fall to the floor. I will carry you the little distance from here to there.*

*

"Don't move, Papa," the older one says. She is nine and serious as a priest. She has decided my arms must be buried too, and she lifts my wrist and lays it back down beside me, arranging, arranging. Her small fingers close around my forearm the way you take up a bone that is still warm.

I let her have the weight of me.

This is what I never understood at the crematorium: that to be lifted is also a gift you give the lifter. My grandmother, in her lightness, taught us the tenderness of our own hands. We learned the softness we were capable of only by holding what could not hold back.

*

The sand comes up over my chest now. My daughters build a mound where my heart is, patting it round, and I feel the cool of the deeper sand and the warm crust the sun has laid on top, two temperatures the way a body has two temperatures at the end, and I think: *someday they will do this for me in earnest.*

They will stand over the tray of me. Someone will name my bones in a language of quiet. *This is the throat that sang to them off-key. This is the little Buddha.* And they will pass me hand to hand, chopstick to chopstick, and I hope they do not weep, I hope instead they feel what I feel now under this weight of sand—

that being covered is not the same as being buried.

That there is a burying which is only love practicing itself. Rehearsing. Getting the hands ready.

*

"There," the younger one announces. Only my face remains. I am a man made of shoreline, breathing through a small opening in the earth. Above me two faces lean in, blotting the sun, laughing, checking their work, and the tide is coming and will unmake all of it before evening, will lift me grain by grain and carry me the little distance from here to there.

I close my eyes.

Let them practice. Let them learn the softness of what they will one day have to lift.

I hold still.
I let myself be light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem about mortality that uses the imagery of the sun as fire, a glass fishing buoy washing ashore, and a Japanese cremation ceremony.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Tide Delivers**

The sun goes down like something set on fire,
a slow combustion at the water's edge,
and I have come to watch the day expire
the way a candle argues with its wick—
each flame a little sermon on the brief.

Here at low tide, a glass float washes in,
a buoy loosed from some forgotten net,
its green sphere clouded, traveled, oceaned-thin,
a bubble blown in Honshu decades back
that crossed the whole Pacific to arrive
as if to prove that nothing is quite lost,
only rerouted, only long in transit.

I think of how my grandmother was burned,
how afterward we gathered at the tray
and lifted her, bone by particular bone,
with chopsticks passed from careful hand to hand—
the ankle first, they said, and then the skull,
so she would not be resting on her head
throughout whatever comes, or does not come.

We placed her in the urn from feet to crown,
rebuilding her in fragments, ash and light,
the body's final architecture drawn
from what the fire had chosen not to keep.

And this is what the tide delivers: forms
that outlast their intentions. The glass sphere.
The sun, that furnace we are orbiting,
that will one day forget to rise for us.
The bone. The float. The self let loose to drift.

I hold the buoy up against the dusk.
The fire behind it fills the hollow green.
For just this moment, something clouded holds
the light entire—then dark, then dark, then dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an evocative poem addressed partly to "Father" that juxtaposes Japanese post-cremation rituals with a tender beach scene of small children and an ocean-borne glass globe.
counterfactuals.output:
**Kotsuage**

Father, they gave us chopsticks made of bamboo and of willow,
one green, one white, and told us to pass you
bone to bone, hand to waiting hand—
the only time such passing is not forbidden.

We began at the feet, the priest said,
so you would not stand on your head in the next world.
Your ankle, small as a river stone.
Your hyoid, the throat's soft harp, they lifted last
and named the Buddha sitting in the lotus of your neck.

*

Meanwhile, somewhere the tide was doing its own arithmetic.

Two children I will never know
crouched at the lip of the Pacific,
and a glass globe rode the swells toward them—
a fishing float slipped from its net
a hundred years and half an ocean ago,
green as bottle-light, furred with salt,
holding nothing but a mouthful of trapped air,
a single breath exhaled by a drowned man
or by no one, by the sea itself.

They did not break it.
They cupped it the way you cup a thing
that has crossed too much water to be dropped,
each small hand offering it to the other—
*here, you hold it, no, you*—
that same careful passing,
that same reluctance to be the one
who lets the fragile weight go down.

*

Father, I want to tell you
the bones came apart like coral,
that you were lighter than the box that held you,
that when we sealed the urn
I understood the globe at last:

how the sea keeps sending back
its round green griefs, intact,
how the vessel matters less than the fact
of arrival, of children on a shore
who have not yet learned
that everything given hand to hand
is on its way, always,
to the ground or to the water—

and still they lift it to the sun.
And still they call it beautiful.
And still, and still, they do not let it fall.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
